title: Does an SR&ED Claim Trigger a CRA Tax Audit? | Canada FAQ
description: Can an SR&ED claim prompt a CRA review? See how Canadian SR&ED claims can lead to CRA technical and financial review of the claim.
summary: For Canadian businesses claiming federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentives, a claim can prompt CRA technical and financial reviews of the work and expenditures. Inconsistencies, such as expensing equipment in the accounting books while claiming it as SR&ED capital property on Form T661, are an immediate audit trigger, so contemporaneous documentation is essential.

Executive Summary and Legislative Architecture of the Canadian SR&ED Regime

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program serves as the cornerstone of Canada's federal innovation policy, supporting more than 24,160 businesses annually through a dual-mechanism fiscal architecture integrated directly into the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). Established in its modern structural form in 1985 and administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and the Department of Finance Canada, the program provides two distinct, interlocking statutory benefits to taxpayers prosecuting qualifying research and development within Canadian jurisdiction. First, subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act permits the immediate deduction or indefinite pooling and carryforward of allowable SR&ED expenditures in computing income from a business. Second, subsections 127(5) and 127(9) provide for the generation of refundable and non-refundable Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) calculated on the claimant's annual "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool".

Between December 2024 and March 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential legislative transformation in over a decade. Following policy proposals introduced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024) and expanded through the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, Parliament fundamentally recalibrated the federal SR&ED incentive structure for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024). These statutory amendments addressed three long-standing structural bottlenecks that had constrained capital-intensive and scaling Canadian technology enterprises since the 2012–2014 federal tax austerity reforms.

The first major pillar of the Bill C-15 reform was the expansion of the enhanced 35% refundable credit ceiling and corporate eligibility criteria. The annual SR&ED expenditure limit governing access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC was ultimately doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000—superseding an initial interim proposal of $4,500,000 announced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement—thereby increasing the maximum annual federal cash refund on current expenditures from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000. Simultaneously, eligibility for this enhanced 35% refundable tier, which had previously been restricted exclusively to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), was extended to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) utilizing a three-year average gross revenue phase-out structure, an election now also made available to CCPCs as an alternative to the prior-year taxable capital test.

The second pillar of the federal reform widened the taxable capital phase-out thresholds for private domestic innovators. For CCPCs utilizing the capital-based expenditure limit test, the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (TCEC) phase-out range across an associated corporate group was expanded from the legacy $10,000,000–$50,000,000 corridor to $15,000,000–$75,000,000. This adjustment preserves the enhanced 35% refundable credit rate for mid-market domestic enterprises that require substantial balance-sheet assets and physical infrastructure to scale their operations.

The third pillar restored capital expenditures to the SR&ED program after an eleven-year hiatus. Effective for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, and lease obligations first becoming payable after December 15, 2024, Parliament reversed the 2014 repeal of paragraph 37(1)(b) and restored capital expenditures—including high-performance artificial intelligence compute infrastructure, graphics processing units (GPUs), laboratory apparatus, pilot plants, and specialized fabrication machinery—to both the section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool for ITC calculation.

Concurrently, provincial jurisdictions executed major structural realignments during the 2025–2026 fiscal cycle to modernize their sub-national innovation frameworks. Most notably, the Government of Quebec used its 2025–2026 Budget, tabled on March 25, 2025, to abolish six legacy R&D and design tax credits—including the foundational Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D)—and consolidate them into the unified Refundable Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. Meanwhile, Ontario (via its 2026 Fall Economic Statement) and British Columbia (via Bill 2, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026) harmonized their provincial R&D tax credit statutes with the federal restoration of capital expenditures and expanded expenditure limits, while Alberta made its incremental Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) a permanent fixture of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act in its 2025 Budget.
Statutory and Regulatory Foundations

The legal authority governing federal R&D tax relief in Canada is codified across three primary sections of the federal Income Tax Act (ITA) and two parts of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). Unlike discretionary grant programs administered by federal or provincial innovation ministries, the SR&ED program operates as a binding statutory entitlement: where a taxpayer satisfies the technical definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1), incurs allowable expenditures under section 37, and files the prescribed forms within the statutory reporting deadline under subsections 37(11) and 127(9), the Minister of National Revenue is legally obligated to recognise the deduction and issue the corresponding tax credit.
The Statutory Definition of SR&ED: Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act establishes the exhaustive legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" for all federal tax purposes and, by statutory incorporation or parallel codification, for provincial R&D tax regimes. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED is defined as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, encompassing three primary categories of investigation alongside a fourth category of directly commensurate support work.

Under paragraph 248(1)(a), the statute recognises basic research, which comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Paragraph 248(1)(b) encompasses applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Paragraph 248(1)(c) covers experimental development, which consists of work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. In Canadian corporate tax practice, experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c) accounts for the vast majority of industrial SR&ED claims across the software, manufacturing, biotechnology, clean technology, and agricultural sectors.

To ensure that ancillary technical activities necessary to execute core experiments are captured within the incentive base, paragraph 248(1)(d) extends the definition of SR&ED to prescribed support work. This provision encompasses work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Crucially, subsection 248(1) also enumerates explicit statutory exclusions in paragraphs (e) through (k), barring specific commercial and routine activities from constituting SR&ED even when performed by qualified scientists or engineers, unless they qualify strictly as commensurate support work under paragraph (d). These statutory exclusions bar market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.
The Deductible Expenditure Pool: Section 37 of the Income Tax Act

Section 37 of the Income Tax Act operates as the computational engine for deducting SR&ED expenditures in computing income from a business carried on by a taxpayer. Rather than requiring taxpayers to capitalize R&D costs or deduct them strictly in the year incurred under general business income principles (section 9 and paragraph 18(1)(a)), subsection 37(1) aggregates qualifying expenditures into a cumulative, non-expiring tax pool. A taxpayer may deduct any portion of the positive balance of its subsection 37(1) pool in a given taxation year to reduce net business income to nil, carrying forward any undeducted balance indefinitely to future taxation years.

body.text: The Investment Tax Credit Mechanism: Section 127 of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

While section 37 governs the deduction of R&D outlays against taxable income, section 127 of the Income Tax Act governs the calculation, application, refundability, transfer, and recapture of the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit. Under subsection 127(9), a claimant's "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" is computed at the end of each taxation year; unlike the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool, the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool is an annual computational base that does not carry over to subsequent taxation years. Instead, the pool immediately generates an ITC for the year, which is either refunded in cash (under section 127.1 for qualifying corporations) or added to the taxpayer's ITC pool under subsections 127(5) and 127(9), where it may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years.

The statutory definitions in subsection 127(9) interact directly with Part XXIX (sections 2900–2903) and Part XLVI (section 4606) of the Income Tax Regulations. Regulation 2900 defines the computational mechanics of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under subsection 2900(4), fixing the notional overhead rate at 55% of the direct SR&ED salary base subject to specific caps on specified employees and overall corporate business expenses, while subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) define "directly attributable" overhead expenditures for claimants electing the Traditional Method. Additionally, subsection 2900(11) prescribes the rules governing "first term shared-use-equipment".

Complementing Regulation 2900, Regulation 2902 enumerates "prescribed expenditures" that are explicitly excluded from the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), even where such outlays are otherwise deductible as ordinary business expenses. These exclusions encompass general administrative salaries, legal and accounting fees, entertainment expenses, advertising or selling expenses, convention expenses, fines or penalties, interest and financing costs, and prescribed capital expenditures under paragraph 2902(b), such as land, buildings, leasehold interests in buildings, and used equipment.
The 2024–2026 Legislative Overhaul: Bill C-15 and the Post-December 15, 2024 Regime

The enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, codified the comprehensive modernization of the federal SR&ED program originally initiated in the federal 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024). Because the transitional provisions bifurcate claims based on whether a corporation's taxation year begins before December 16, 2024, or after December 15, 2024—and, with respect to capital property, whether the asset was acquired after December 15, 2024—tax auditors and corporate claimants must maintain rigorous chronological cutoff controls across straddling fiscal periods.
Legislative Evolution from the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Bill C-15

Understanding the legislative trajectory between December 2024 and March 2026 is essential when auditing corporate tax provisions and evaluating secondary commentary. In the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement, the Department of Finance initially proposed raising the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. However, in subsequent legislative drafting consummated in the 2025 Budget and enacted via Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, Parliament expanded this enhancement further, increasing the annual expenditure limit from $4,500,000 to $6,000,000, retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Consequently, for all taxation years commencing on or after December 16, 2024, the operative statutory expenditure limit is $6,000,000.

body.text: Expansion to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Historically, a severe structural distortion in Canadian corporate tax law occurred whenever a domestic technology or life sciences company executed an initial public offering (IPO) on the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX), TSX Venture Exchange, or a foreign stock exchange, or became controlled by public shareholders: the company immediately lost its CCPC status under subsection 125(7) of the Income Tax Act. Upon losing CCPC status, its federal SR&ED ITC rate dropped precipitously from 35% (100% refundable) to 15% (0% refundable). For pre-revenue or clinical-stage public biotechnology, cleantech, and hardware companies without Part I tax payable, the loss of refundability transformed the SR&ED program from a vital non-dilutive cash-flow mechanism into deferred tax assets trapped on the balance sheet.

Under the Bill C-15 framework, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) can now earn the enhanced 35% refundable ITC on up to $6,000,000 of annual qualified expenditures—with 100% refundability on current expenditures and 40% refundability on capital expenditures, plus 40% refundability on the 15% ITC earned above the expenditure limit—for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. To qualify as an ECPC, a corporation must be resident in Canada throughout the taxation year, have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange in Canada (or have elected to be a public corporation), and not be controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons.

Because public corporations frequently raise substantial equity capital that inflates their balance-sheet taxable capital without generating immediate commercial revenue, the statute evaluates ECPC size using a three-year average annual gross revenue test rather than taxable capital. Where the ECPC is a member of a consolidated corporate group that prepares consolidated financial statements, the expenditure limit must be shared among all group members, and the average annual revenue is calculated using the annual revenue reflected in the consolidated financial statements of the group over the preceding three fiscal years. If an entity joins or leaves the consolidated group during the year, the average annual revenue utilized is that of the consolidated group as reflected in its consolidated financial statements for the year in question, treating the group members as a single economic entity.

Furthermore, to ensure competitive parity between private and public innovators, any CCPC may now formally elect for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, to determine its expenditure limit using this identical three-year average annual gross revenue phase-out structure rather than the prior-year taxable capital test. Where a CCPC is associated with other corporations, the gross revenue calculation requires aggregating the total average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of each corporation that is a member of the associated group for the taxation year in question over the preceding three fiscal years, regardless of whether the corporations were associated during the entirety of that three-year period. This election provides major relief for venture-backed CCPCs and capital-intensive hardware startups whose equity or debt financing pushes their taxable capital employed in Canada above $15,000,000 while their gross commercial revenues remain below the revenue phase-out threshold.
Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Expenditure Limits, Refundability, and Carryforward Mechanics
The Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formula (Taxable Capital Method)

For CCPCs that do not elect the gross revenue method, the maximum $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit (for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) is reduced on a straight-line basis once the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (TCEC)—calculated on T2 Schedule 33 (Taxable Capital Employed in Canada – Large Corporations) or Schedule 34 for the corporation and all associated CCPCs—reaches $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated once prior-year TCEC reaches $75,000,000.
Expressed mathematically, for a CCPC (and its associated corporate group) in a taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024, the reduced expenditure limit is determined by the formula:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year TCEC is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year TCEC exceeds $15,000,000.
By comparison, for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the legacy expenditure limit phased out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year TCEC:

Expenditure limit = $3,000,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year TCEC is $10,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year TCEC exceeds $10,000,000.

Tax auditors should note that the historical dual phase-out mechanism—which previously reduced a CCPC's SR&ED expenditure limit when prior-year taxable income of the associated group lay between $500,000 and $800,000—was repealed by Parliament for all taxation years ending after March 18, 2019. Consequently, profitable CCPCs with high active business income suffer no reduction to their SR&ED expenditure limit provided their prior-year TCEC remains below $15,000,000 (or they qualify under the elective gross revenue test). Where a CCPC has a short taxation year (fewer than 51 weeks) or has multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year while associated in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC that has a taxation year ending in that same calendar year, specific proration rules apply, and the expenditure limit must be allocated among associated corporations using T2 Schedule 49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit).

body.text: Carryback, Carryforward, and Taxation of Federal ITCs

When a claimant earns non-refundable ITCs (or elects not to claim a refund where applicable, after offsetting current-year Part I tax payable under subsection 127(5)), the unused federal ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years to recover federal Part I taxes paid in prior periods, or carried forward up to 20 taxation years to offset future federal Part I income tax liabilities.

A fundamental structural principle of the Canadian SR&ED system is that federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credits are themselves subject to taxation in the taxation year following the year in which they are claimed, regardless of whether they are utilized to offset Part I tax payable or received as a cash refund. Specifically, under paragraph 37(1)(e) of the Income Tax Act, the amount of any federal SR&ED ITC claimed by the taxpayer in the preceding taxation year reduces the taxpayer's subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the current taxation year. If the current-year subsection 37(1) pool balance is insufficient to absorb the prior-year federal ITC—as routinely occurs when a taxpayer deducts its entire section 37 pool balance each year—the negative excess is brought directly into the taxpayer's taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(t) of the Income Tax Act. Auditors must observe the critical timing distinction between provincial assistance and federal ITCs: whereas provincial R&D tax credits and direct grants constitute "government assistance" that reduces the subsection 37(1) pool and subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool in the exact same taxation year the expenditures are incurred, the federal SR&ED ITC is taxed one year in arrears via paragraph 37(1)(e) and paragraph 12(1)(t).
Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methodologies, and Capital Property Restoration

To be included in a claimant's "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, an outlay must be incurred in the taxation year in respect of SR&ED carried on in Canada (subject to the 10% foreign salary exception), related to a business of the claimant, and fall within one of the statutory expenditure categories: direct salaries and wages, materials consumed or transformed, arm's-length contract expenditures and third-party payments, overhead expenses (via the Traditional or Proxy Method), or post-December 15, 2024 capital and lease expenditures.
Direct Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, and the 10% Foreign Salary Rule

Salaries and wages paid to employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED represent the largest expenditure component of Canadian R&D claims. The CRA distinguishes between directly engaged employees—such as scientists, engineers, software developers, laboratory technicians, and hands-on first-line technical supervisors whose time is directly required by the technical execution of basic research, applied research, experimental development, or paragraph 248(1)(d) support work—and indirect administrative, human resources, or clerical personnel.

Three strict statutory constraints govern the inclusion of salaries and wages in the SR&ED expenditure base. The first constraint is the 180-day unpaid remuneration rule under subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act. Any salary, wages, or bonus accrued at the end of a taxation year must be actually paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year. If an accrued bonus or wage remains unpaid on the 181st day following fiscal year-end, subsection 78(4) deems the expenditure not to have been incurred in the taxation year; furthermore, while the expense becomes deductible for general corporate income tax purposes when eventually paid in a subsequent year, it is permanently disqualified from SR&ED treatment if not paid within 180 days of the end of the taxation year in which the SR&ED work was performed.

The second constraint governs "specified employees," defined under subsection 248(1) as any employee who is a specified shareholder of the employer—owning, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or any related corporation—or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer. For specified employees, bonuses and remuneration based on profits are 100% excluded from SR&ED salaries and wages, and total claimable SR&ED salary is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days the individual was a specified employee and allocated across associated corporations. Moreover, when computing the salary base for the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under the Proxy Method (Regulation 2900(4)), each specified employee's inclusion in the proxy salary base (Line 818 of Form T661) is further restricted to the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total salary and wages (excluding bonuses and taxable benefits) and 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated for short taxation years and the percentage of time devoted to SR&ED.

The third constraint is the 10% permissible foreign SR&ED salary rule under subsection 37(1.4) and paragraph 37(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act. While SR&ED must generally be carried on within the geographic boundaries of Canada—which statutorily includes Canada's exclusive economic zone, the airspace above that zone, and the seabed and subsoil below that zone within the meaning of the Oceans Act—subsection 37(1.4) permits a taxpayer to claim salaries and wages paid to an employee who is resident in Canada for SR&ED carried on outside Canada, provided four cumulative statutory conditions are met: first, the work was carried on outside Canada; second, the work was directly undertaken by the taxpayer, meaning foreign subcontractors never qualify under this rule; third, the work related to a business of the taxpayer; and fourth, the work was solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer, such as specialized climatic testing or foreign facility trials unavailable domestically. The total claimable foreign SR&ED salary under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) is strictly capped at 10% of the total salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer in the year. Importantly, these foreign salaries cannot be included in the Line 818 salary base used to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount.
Overhead Allocation: Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method

For each taxation year, a claimant must irrevocably elect on Form T661 whether to compute its SR&ED expenditures under the Traditional Method (paragraph 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)) or the Proxy Method (paragraph 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)). Once the income tax return and Form T661 are filed for a taxation year, the election between the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method cannot be revoked or amended for that year.

body.text: Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

Under subparagraphs 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (II) (Traditional Method) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method), a claimant may include the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials consumed refer to physical substances that are rendered virtually valueless or destroyed as a direct consequence of the SR&ED activity, such as chemical reagents, test wafers, destructive testing coupons, and laboratory consumables. By contrast, materials transformed refer to materials that are integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, custom product, or commercial asset during the SR&ED process where the resulting body of matter retains commercial value or utility at the conclusion of testing. For property that a claimant manufactures for its own use, eligible cost includes material, labour, and overhead costs reasonably attributable to the property, but excludes any notional profit that might have been earned had the property been sold.

While both consumed and transformed materials qualify initially at 100% of their cost in the subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9) pools, materials transformed are subject to the ITC Recapture Rules under subsection 127(27) if the resulting prototype, custom product, experimental production, or commercial production with experimental development is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years. Furthermore, supplies that are neither physically incorporated into the experimental prototype nor destroyed in testing—such as hand tools, protective eyewear, or cleaning fluids—do not qualify as materials for SR&ED; instead, they are treated as overhead, meaning they are absorbed within the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method or claimed as directly attributable overhead under the Traditional Method.
Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Performers, and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant outsources R&D activities or funds external research, the tax treatment depends strictly on two legal distinctions: first, whether the payment is a contract expenditure for SR&ED performed on behalf of the claimant versus a third-party payment; and second, whether the performer deals at arm's length with the claimant.

Where a claimant engages an arm's-length contractor to perform SR&ED work in Canada on the claimant's behalf under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and subsection 127(9)—meaning the claimant defines the technical specifications, bears the financial risk, and retains ownership or exploitation rights to the resulting intellectual property—100% of the contract payment is deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool, but only 80% of the expenditure is included in the subsection 127(9) "qualified expenditure" pool for federal ITC calculation. This statutory 20% reduction eliminates the contractor's presumed commercial profit markup from the federal tax credit base. The former capital look-through rule in subsection 37(14), which required the payer to allocate the price of an arm's-length contract combining SR&ED work with commercial deliverables or capital property across its constituent elements, was repealed by S.C. 2026, c. 3, s. 5 (Bill C-15).

By contrast, third-party payments under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) encompass payments made to an approved university, college, research institute, or other similar approved organization (or to an agricultural organization check-off fund, or to a taxable Canadian corporation under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1) for basic or applied research) where the claimant does not direct the day-to-day execution of the research (that is, the work is not performed "on behalf of" the claimant). Such third-party payments qualify if the SR&ED is carried on in Canada, relates to a business of the claimant, and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED in its business as a direct result of the payment. For third-party payments made to a Canadian-resident corporation ("A entity"), an additional statutory condition requires that the primary purpose of the payment be for the claimant to use the results from the basic or applied research in conjunction with other SR&ED undertaken or to be undertaken, directly by or on behalf of the claimant, that relates to a business of the claimant. Note that under subsection 37(2), payments to an approved foreign university, college, or research institute for SR&ED carried on outside Canada may be deducted in computing business income if the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results, but such foreign payments do not earn SR&ED Investment Tax Credits. Domestic third-party payments are 100% deductible under subsection 37(1) and included at 80% in the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes, and must be reported on Form T1263 (Schedule 30) (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED).

Where SR&ED work is outsourced to a related company, paragraphs (f) and (g) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) exclude payments made to a person or partnership with whom the claimant does not deal at arm's length from the payer's qualified expenditures (0% eligible to the payer directly). Instead, subsection 37(13) deems work performed by a taxpayer for a non-arm's-length person or partnership to be SR&ED where it would be SR&ED if performed directly by that person or partnership. The non-arm's-length performer computes its own underlying qualified SR&ED expenditures (salaries, materials, PPA, and 80% of its own arm's-length subcontracts) without reduction for the intercompany contract payment, and the two related parties may execute a prescribed Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures (Form T1146) under subsection 127(13) to transfer the qualified expenditures from the performer to the payer, capped at the actual intercompany contract amount paid. Furthermore, where a claimant purchases goods or non-R&D services from a non-arm's-length supplier that are subsequently used in SR&ED, the expenditure is restricted to the actual cost incurred by the non-arm's-length supplier to provide the property or service.
Restoration of Capital Expenditures and Leased Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024 Rules)

From January 1, 2014, through December 15, 2024, capital expenditures and capital lease obligations were entirely barred from both section 37 deductibility and section 127 ITC eligibility. Under the revised CRA Capital Expenditures Policy aligned with Bill C-15, depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024—and lease payments that first become payable after December 15, 2024—once again qualify for both full immediate write-off under paragraph 37(1)(b) (deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance under subsection 37(6)) and federal SR&ED ITCs under subsection 127(9).

To audit and substantiate post-December 15, 2024 SR&ED capital expenditures, claimants must satisfy rigorous statutory thresholds across both the Traditional Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III)) and the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III)). The primary pathway is the 90% All-or-Substantially-All (ASA) Test: at the time the capital expenditure is incurred, the claimant must establish an objective intention that the depreciable property will either be used during all or substantially all (defined by the CRA as 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada, or have all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada, such as custom test rigs or pilot apparatus whose structural value is exhausted during experimental trials. Qualifying ASA capital assets purchased after December 15, 2024, include high-performance GPU clusters and servers for artificial intelligence and machine learning model development, laboratory instruments, cameras, drones and recording gear used in testing, specialized fabrication machinery, and industrial sensors used in R&D processes.

Where new depreciable machinery or equipment does not meet the 90% ASA threshold over its entire useful life, but is used "primarily"—defined as more than 50% and less than 90% of its operating time—for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada during its initial operating periods, it may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under the definitions of "first term shared-use-equipment" and "second term shared-use-equipment" in subsection 127(9) and Regulation 2900(11). Under the SUE rules, a claimant earns an ITC on 25% (one-quarter) of the capital cost in the "first term" (the period ending 12 months after the property was acquired and became available for use) and an additional 25% (one-quarter) of the capital cost in the "second term" (the period ending 24 months after acquisition and available-for-use status), provided actual SR&ED operating usage exceeds 50% in each respective term. Once property has been claimed as shared-use equipment for two years, it is no longer eligible for further SR&ED credits, capping the cumulative qualified expenditure inclusion at 50% of the equipment's capital cost. Depreciable property used less than 50% of its operating time on SR&ED is completely ineligible (0%) for SR&ED tax incentives.

Similar proportional rules govern leased equipment for lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024. Equipment leased by a claimant that is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada qualifies at 100% of the lease payments. Where leased equipment (other than general-purpose office equipment or furniture) is used primarily—between 50% and 90% of its operating time—for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, 50% (one-half) of the lease cost is eligible under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(VI).

Several strict exclusions and accounting consistency mandates apply to all SR&ED capital claims. First, only brand-new equipment that has never been used, or acquired for use or lease, for any purpose whatsoever before it was acquired by the claimant qualifies for the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit under subsection 127(9); used or refurbished equipment may qualify for the subsection 37(1)(b) deduction pool if it satisfies the 90% ASA test, but is strictly barred from earning an ITC. Second, statutorily excluded assets—including land, buildings, leasehold interests in buildings (paragraph 37(8)(d) and Regulation 2902(b)), payments made to an approved university, college, or organization to enable the recipient to acquire a building or leasehold interest in a building (subparagraph 37(8)(d)(iv)), general-purpose office equipment or furniture (desks, chairs, filing cabinets, photocopiers, fax machines, telephones), motor vehicles, tools used mainly for day-to-day commercial production, and commercial inventory items—cannot be claimed as SR&ED capital property. Third, under subsection 13(27) and the CRA Capital Expenditures Policy, capital property cannot be claimed until the taxation year in which it is both acquired and available for use. Finally, to claim an asset as SR&ED capital property, the corporation must record the asset as depreciable capital property on its balance sheet for financial reporting and tax purposes; recording equipment as a current expense in the accounting books while claiming it as a depreciable capital asset on Form T661 is an immediate CRA audit trigger. Claimants must maintain purchase invoices, delivery slips supporting available-for-use dates, and contemporaneous equipment usage logbooks recording the date of each use, the project or activity, the operator, the approximate hours or percentage of the day used, and whether the usage was for SR&ED or commercial activity.
Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and ITC Recapture Rules
Reduction of Pool Balances by Assistance and Contract Payments

To prevent the double-dipping of public subsidies or the claiming of tax credits on work already funded by commercial customers in Canada, paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9) (paragraph (h) of "qualified expenditure"), 127(18), 127(19), and 127(20) mandate that a claimant's SR&ED deductible expenditure pool and SR&ED qualified expenditure pool be reduced by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year.

Under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x), "government assistance" encompasses assistance from any federal, provincial, territorial, municipal, or foreign government, municipality, or other public authority—whether in the form of a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance—including funding distributed through a non-profit organization that in turn receives its funding from a government organization (such as NRC IRAP, provincial R&D tax credits, and any GST/HST input tax credit or rebate received for property acquired). Similarly, "non-government assistance" under paragraph 12(1)(x) and subsection 127(9) includes any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, allowance, or other form of inducement or assistance received from a non-public entity in respect of the SR&ED.

A "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) and Regulation 4606 is defined either as an amount paid or payable to a claimant by a "taxable supplier" (a person or partnership resident in Canada or carrying on business through a permanent establishment in Canada) in respect of SR&ED performed for, or on behalf of, a person or partnership entitled to a deduction for the amount as a current expenditure under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) or as a third-party payment to a corporation under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1) at a time when the claimant and the taxable supplier are dealing at arm's length, or as an amount for a current SR&ED expenditure (other than a prescribed amount under Regulation 4606) payable by a Canadian government, municipality, other Canadian public authority, or person exempt from Part I tax under section 149 for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf. In evaluating whether an amount is a contract payment, the CRA examines the legal substance of the commercial contract rather than merely its label. This mechanism ensures that when a Canadian payer hires an arm's-length Canadian performer to conduct SR&ED on the payer's behalf, the payer claims the SR&ED ITC (on 80% of the contract expenditure), while the performer must reduce its own qualified SR&ED expenditures by the contract payment received from the payer so that both entities cannot claim duplicate ITCs on the same research work.

When the total amount of government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments relating to a specific project exceeds the SR&ED expenditures of that project, subsections 127(19) and 127(20) require the excess assistance to be allocated across non-arm's-length members of a group performing the same SR&ED, reducing their qualified SR&ED expenditures down to nil. Conversely, if a taxpayer subsequently repays government or non-government assistance that previously reduced its qualified expenditures, paragraph 37(1)(c) adds the repaid amount to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool and paragraphs (e.1) and (e.2) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), alongside subsections 127(10.7) and 127(10.8), generate a corresponding addition to the taxpayer's ITC pool.
Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(35))

Whenever a corporation disposes of a property on which it previously claimed an SR&ED ITC—or converts that property to commercial use—within 20 years of the original acquisition, the ITC Recapture Rules under subsections 127(27), 127(29), and 127(34) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA Recapture of Investment Tax Credit Policy trigger a direct clawback of the tax credit, which is added directly to federal Part I tax payable on Line 602 of the T2 return (and calculated in Parts 16, 17, and 24 of Schedule 31). Furthermore, with the restoration of capital expenditures after December 15, 2024, selling or converting SR&ED capital property to commercial use affects both the capital cost allowance claimed and unclaimed SR&ED capital expenditures, in addition to triggering SR&ED ITC recapture.

The categories of property subject to SR&ED ITC recapture include materials for SR&ED that are transformed and included in a custom product, a commercial asset, experimental production, or commercial production with experimental development; post-December 15, 2024 all-or-substantially-all (ASA) capital equipment; shared-use equipment (SUE); animals and other growing things used in SR&ED projects; and property acquired through a contract involving SR&ED and other work. In computing the cost of a property for recapture purposes, the cost excludes any amount paid by the claimant to maintain, modify, or transform the property, and excludes internal salaries, wages, or overhead costs that might otherwise be imputed by the claimant to the cost of the property.

For an arm's-length disposition or conversion to commercial use under subsection 127(27), the recapture amount added to Part I tax payable on Line 602 is the lesser of two figures: first, the actual SR&ED ITC originally earned by the taxpayer for the property; and second, the amount determined by applying the percentage rate that the taxpayer used in calculating the ITC earned on the property (such as 35% or 15%) to the proceeds of disposition of the property (if disposed of to an arm's-length person) or, in any other case (such as conversion to commercial use or a non-arm's-length disposition), to the fair market value of the property.

Where the taxpayer performed the SR&ED and transferred the qualified expenditures to a non-arm's-length party pursuant to an agreement under subsection 127(13), subsection 127(29) mandates that the recapture is the lesser of the ITC earned by the transferee on the qualified expenditures for the transferred property, and the amount determined by the statutory formula A × B − C, where A is the percentage rate that the transferee used in determining its ITC, B is the proceeds of disposition (if sold at arm's length) or the fair market value of the property (in any other case), and C is the amount, if any, already added to tax payable under subsection 127(27) for the property (which addresses situations where only a portion of the cost was transferred under subsection 127(13)). Note that a timing complication arises if the performer disposes of the property, transfers the qualified expenditure to a non-arm's-length payer, and the payer's taxation year-end precedes the performer's taxation year-end.

Crucially, the CRA Recapture of Investment Tax Credit Policy confirms that intellectual property (IP) generated during an SR&ED project does not trigger ITC recapture when sold or licensed. Where the rights to IP belong to the payer under the terms of an R&D contract, the payer is not acquiring a physical property from the performer; the IP simply accrues to the payer as it is generated, so there is no recapture if the payer subsequently sells or leases the IP rights. Similarly, if the IP rights rest with the performer under an initial $100,000 SR&ED contract (which qualifies as an allowable SR&ED expenditure for the payer), and the payer subsequently pays $20,000 under a separate contract at the end of the project to purchase the IP rights from the performer, that $20,000 payment is barred from SR&ED deduction under subsection 37(4) as a payment to acquire rights in or arising out of SR&ED, and the performer does not suffer ITC recapture on the sale of the IP.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes (2025–2026 Landscape)

Most Canadian provinces and the Yukon Territory operate statutory R&D tax credits or tax-system grants that stack atop the federal SR&ED program. Because provincial R&D tax credits and Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the federal Income Tax Act, the dollar amount of the provincial credit earned in a taxation year must be deducted from the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool before the federal 35% or 15% ITC is computed.

body.text: Deep Dive 1: Quebec's 2025–2026 Budget Overhaul and the New CRIC Regime

Quebec operates an autonomous corporate income tax administration through Revenu Québec under the Taxation Act (Quebec) and the Act respecting the sectoral parameters of certain fiscal measures. Historically, Quebec maintained a fragmented array of six specialized R&D and design tax credits, under which rates could reach up to 37.5% or 30% depending on the claimant's asset size and research structure. In the 2025–2026 Quebec Budget tabled on March 25, 2025, the Quebec government executed a sweeping consolidation of its fiscal innovation incentives. Effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec abolished six legacy tax credit regimes: first, the Refundable Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D); second, the Tax Credit for University Research and for Research Carried on by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium; third, the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research; fourth, the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium; fifth, the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services; and sixth, the industrial design component of the Tax Credit for an In-House Design Activity (while leaving the fashion design component unchanged). Under transitional rules, an eligible fee balance of a taxpayer or partnership at the end of a taxation year or fiscal period ending after March 25, 2025, can continue to generate the legacy consortium R&D tax credit under the same terms for a taxation year ending on or before December 31, 2029, and the Act respecting the sectoral parameters of certain fiscal measures was amended so that the Minister of the Economy, Innovation and Energy continues to issue certificates of recognition for eligible public research centres and eligible research consortia for purposes of the new regime.

To replace those six abolished credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec established the Refundable Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization, known by its French acronym as the CRIC. The CRIC provides a two-tier, 100% refundable tax credit structure: it delivers an enhanced 30% refundable rate on up to $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the exclusion threshold (shared among members of an associated corporate group), and a 20% refundable rate on all qualified expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 ceiling. Transitional eligibility rules also address corporations whose assets shown in their financial statements were less than $50,000,000 and to which an amount under one of the former R&D tax credits was granted or allocated for a taxation year ended in 2025 or one of the three preceding taxation years.

A major policy innovation of the CRIC is its explicit expansion beyond classic R&D to encompass pre-commercialization activities that continue R&D carried out in Quebec. Qualifying pre-commercialization work includes tests and studies conducted to obtain an initial registration or regulatory certification required to commercialize a product or process, as well as product design activities. Because the federal SR&ED program does not cover post-R&D regulatory certification or commercial product design unless those activities simultaneously resolve a technological uncertainty under subsection 248(1), pre-commercialization expenditures that do not meet the federal SR&ED definition appear exclusively in the Quebec CRIC claim and do not reduce the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool as government assistance.

Furthermore, the 2025–2026 Quebec Budget standardized the eligible expenditure base under the CRIC across three cost categories. First, direct salaries for R&D and pre-commercialization work carried out in Quebec qualify at 100%. Second, capital expenditures (CAPEX for equipment only) acquired for R&D or pre-commercialization in Quebec qualify at 100% of eligible amounts, subject to limitations where property is used as part of a large investment project benefiting from a tax holiday. Third, subcontracting contracts—whether awarded to private R&D service providers, universities, College Centres for the Transfer of Technologies (CCTTs), public research centres, or research consortia—are standardized and reduced to a single uniform inclusion rate of 50% of eligible amounts.

Before applying the 30% and 20% CRIC rates, the claimant must subtract an annual exclusion threshold from its eligible Quebec expenditures. Under the CRIC rules, the exclusion threshold is equal to the greater of $50,000 and the sum of the R&D employees threshold plus the pre-commercialization employees threshold. Notably, while the exclusion threshold reduces the expenditure base eligible for the CRIC, the Quebec nexus ratio used to calculate the Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations in Quebec (DICI)—Quebec's preferential tax regime for intellectual property commercialization—is not reduced by the CRIC exclusion threshold. To claim the CRIC, corporations file Form RD-222 (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures) and the prescribed CRIC schedules with their Quebec corporate income tax return, maintaining a unified project list and employee time records that reconcile the Quebec and federal bases.
Deep Dive 2: Ontario's Dual-Credit System (OITC and ORDTC)

Ontario administers two complementary corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) that are harmonized with federal SR&ED eligibility and claimed via schedules filed with the T2 corporate income tax return. The first incentive is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), which provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit to qualifying corporations on eligible SR&ED expenditures carried out in Ontario. The second incentive is the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), which provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit to corporations conducting qualifying SR&ED in Ontario.

In computing the two Ontario credits, the 8% refundable OITC is calculated first on qualifying Ontario SR&ED expenditures, and the resulting OITC amount reduces the qualified expenditure base eligible for the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC. Subsequently, both the OITC and the ORDTC (unless formally waived) constitute government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, reducing the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool prior to the calculation of the 35% or 15% federal ITC. In the 2026 Ontario Fall Economic Statement, the Government of Ontario confirmed that eligibility for qualifying capital expenditures under both the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit and the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit was restored for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, effective automatically when the federal legislation received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, aligning Ontario's provincial R&D tax base with the federal Bill C-15 capital expenditure restoration.
Deep Dive 3: British Columbia's Harmonized 10% Credit (Bill 2, 2026)

Under Part 6 of the Income Tax Act (B.C.) and Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), the Province of British Columbia provides a 10% SR&ED tax credit on SR&ED qualified BC expenditures incurred by a qualifying corporation with a permanent establishment in British Columbia. Through Bill 2 (2026), British Columbia fully aligned its provincial SR&ED credit with the federal Bill C-15 reforms effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024.

Under the harmonized BC rules, qualifying corporations that are either CCPCs or Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) may claim a 10% refundable tax credit on the lesser of the corporation's SR&ED qualified BC expenditure for the taxation year or the federal expenditure limit, which is increased to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Furthermore, British Columbia increased the prior-year taxable capital phase-out threshold for determining a CCPC's expenditure limit to $15,000,000, phasing out completely once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000, and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures as BC qualified expenditures. All qualifying corporations (including large corporations and CCPCs/ECPCs with BC expenditures exceeding their refundable limit) may claim a 10% non-refundable BC SR&ED tax credit on their SR&ED qualified BC expenditures for the year less the amount of their refundable BC credit and any amount renounced for that year. To claim the credit, corporations must file Form T666 (British Columbia (BC) Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit) and enter the non-refundable credit on Line 659 and the refundable credit on Line 674 of T2 Schedule 5 (Tax Calculation Supplementary – Corporations) no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the qualified expenditures are incurred.
Deep Dive 4: Alberta's Permanent Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Unlike Ontario and British Columbia, Alberta administers its own corporate income tax system through the Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, maintaining an 8% general corporate income tax rate (23% combined federal-Alberta general rate) and a 2% small business rate (11% combined rate) confirmed in the 2025 Alberta Budget. Following the elimination of the former Alberta SR&ED tax credit effective January 1, 2020, Alberta introduced the refundable Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) under section 26.6 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act for eligible R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020. In the 2025 Alberta Budget (tabled February 27, 2025), the provincial government removed the program's sunset clause and made the IEG a permanent structural component of Alberta's tax code.

Delivered directly through the corporate tax system without requiring a pre-application, the IEG provides qualified corporations that have a permanent establishment in Alberta with a two-tier refundable payment on up to $4,000,000 in annual R&D spending matching federal SR&ED qualified expenditures under section 37 and Regulation 2900 carried out in Alberta. First, the corporation receives an 8% base payment on eligible R&D spending carried out in Alberta up to the corporation's base level of spending, which is determined by calculating the corporation's average qualifying R&D spending over the preceding two taxation years. Second, the corporation receives an enhanced 20% incremental payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds its two-year average base spending level, up to the $4,000,000 annual expenditure cap (yielding a maximum annual refundable grant of up to $800,000).

Mathematically, for an Alberta claimant with current-year eligible Alberta R&D spending E (capped at the maximum expenditure limit L, which is $4,000,000 for corporations with prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of $10,000,000 or less) and prior two-year average Alberta R&D spending B, the total refundable IEG is:
IEG = 8% × min(E′, B) + 20% × max(0, E′ − B), where E′ = min(E, L).

Per official Government of Alberta guidelines and the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, the IEG phases out incrementally for firms with between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada, and firms with $50,000,000 or more in taxable capital are completely ineligible for the grant. Claimants file AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29), AT1 Schedule 13, and Form AT4970 (Listing of SR&ED Projects Carried Out in Alberta) with their Alberta AT1 return, with typical TRA processing times of 6 to 9 months from filing. Any excess credit over Alberta tax payable is refunded in cash, and the IEG is included in federal taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(x) and treated as government assistance.
Technological Eligibility Jurisprudence: From Northwest Hydraulic to Canafric Inc. v. The King

Because the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) turns on qualitative scientific and engineering concepts ("systematic investigation or search," "experiment or analysis," and "technological advancement"), Canadian tax courts have developed a rigorous body of jurisprudence that governs all CRA technical reviews.
The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998)

In the landmark decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839 (Tax Court of Canada)—subsequently affirmed as the binding interpretation of subsection 248(1) by the Federal Court of Appeal in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72—the Tax Court established the five foundational criteria (the "Five Questions") for determining whether an activity constitutes SR&ED.

The first question asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Where a technical problem can be resolved through standard engineering calculations, published reference manuals, or routine debugging by competent professionals in the field, no technological uncertainty exists. The second question asks whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. The third question asks whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses through systematic experiment or analysis rather than ad hoc trial-and-error. The fourth question asks whether the process resulted in a technological advancement—that is, an advancement in technical knowledge that was not previously available in the public domain or to competent professionals, including the rejection of a hypothesis that proves why a specific approach cannot work under given constraints. Finally, the fifth question asks whether a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results was kept as the work progressed.
The CRA's Administrative Consolidation: The "Why" and "How" Framework

In August 2021, the CRA archived its former Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (which explicitly structured reviews around the five Northwest Hydraulic questions) and replaced it with its updated Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives. The CRA guidelines distil the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) into two overarching requirements—the "Why" and the "How"—while emphasizing that both the two requirements and the five questions derive from the unchanged text of subsection 248(1).

Under the "Why" requirement, the CRA evaluates why the work is being conducted: specifically, whether it is undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge (basic or applied research) or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement (experimental development), as opposed to achieving commercial product differentiation or business goals. Under the "How" requirement, the CRA evaluates how the work is conducted: whether it proceeds by means of a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The CRA's "How" framework requires four operational elements: the generation of a hypothesis (an idea consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward resolving a technological problem); the testing of this idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis (recognising that the hypothesis can evolve and change as a result of testing); the development of logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis; and the keeping of evidence that is generated as the work progresses.

body.text: Judicial Rebukes to Administrative Overreach: National R&D and Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023)

Following the introduction of the CRA's updated administrative guidelines, the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed in National R&D that while the CRA's administrative policies are useful tools, the binding legal interpretation of the SR&ED definition in subsection 248(1) remains the common-law test set out in Northwest Hydraulic. Subsequently, on July 26, 2023, the Tax Court of Canada issued its landmark ruling in Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108 (Dockets 2018-677(IT)G, 2019-3835(IT)G, 2020-1571(IT)G and 2020-1574(IT)G), allowing the appeals in full and upholding the SR&ED expenditures and investment tax credits claimed by Canafric Inc. for its 2013, 2014, 2015 and 2016 taxation years, and reaffirming the primacy of the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria over overly rigid administrative formalism. Canafric confirmed that industrial experimental development conducted in a commercial production environment satisfies the Northwest Hydraulic framework where the claimant systematically formulates and tests hypotheses to overcome genuine technological uncertainties and achieves incremental technological advancements, even when the contemporaneous records take the form of practical industrial trial logs rather than academic treatises.
Administrative Compliance, Prescribed Forms, Statutory Deadlines, and Audit Defence Protocols
Prescribed Filing Forms and Line-by-Line Architecture

To claim federal SR&ED deductions and Investment Tax Credits, a corporate taxpayer must file two mandatory prescribed forms with its T2 Corporation Income Tax Return: Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, also referenced as Schedule 32 in corporate tax software) and Schedule T2SCH31 (Schedule 31) (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations). Since January 1, 2016, the CRA has required the standardized T661(15) or later prescribed version of Form T661 for all taxation years. Unincorporated individuals and trusts file Form T661 alongside Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)), while claimants making third-party payments must also attach Form T1263 (Schedule 30) (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED). Where a project involves classified national security information, the claimant completes Form T661 using a separate sheet for Section B of Part 2, includes a copy of the official classification letter with the return, and retains the classified Section B narrative on file rather than transmitting it with the return.

The Strict 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline and Penalties

Under subsections 37(11) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, eligibility for an SR&ED deduction and Investment Tax Credit is strictly limited to those expenditures identified on Form T661 and Schedule 31 filed within 12 months of the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenses were made or incurred (determined without reference to subsection 78(4)). Because a corporation's T2 filing-due date is 6 months after its taxation year-end, adding 12 months creates an absolute statutory SR&ED reporting deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year. For example, for a corporate taxation year ended December 31, 2024, the absolute statutory deadline is June 30, 2026. The CRA does not grant administrative extensions to this 18-month bar except in narrow statutory circumstances. Furthermore, where a third-party consultant or preparer assists in preparing Form T661, complete claim preparer information must be reported in Part 8 of Form T661; if claim preparer information is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a mandatory $1,000 penalty applies, alongside potential negligence and third-party civil penalties for false statements.
Strategic Capital Allocation, Grant Stacking, and Multi-Jurisdictional Optimization
The "Proxy Shield" Stacking Multiplier: Combining NRC IRAP with SR&ED

Canada's innovation ecosystem enables corporations to stack direct non-repayable salary grants—most notably from the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which covers up to 80% of internal technical R&D labour and provides a median contribution of $75,000 (with the middle half of awards ranging from $50,000 to $194,900)—alongside provincial and federal R&D tax credits. When a claimant elects the Proxy Method on Form T661, an NRC IRAP grant reimbursing direct SR&ED salaries creates a highly advantageous "Proxy Shield" effect. Because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 820) is computed directly on the unreduced eligible SR&ED salary base (Line 818) before government assistance is deducted on Lines 429 and 513, the claimant earns federal and provincial SR&ED tax credits not only on the unsubsidized portion of its R&D salaries, but also on the entire 55% notional overhead proxy generated by the IRAP-funded salaries.

Synthesis and Audit Compliance Conclusions

To maximize non-dilutive recovery while maintaining full audit defensibility under the post-Bill C-15 Canadian R&D tax architecture, corporate claimants and tax auditors must implement five core operational controls. First, organizations must enforce strict chronological cutoff accounting around the December 15, 2024 statutory transition date—verifying both the start date of the taxation year for the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, ECPC eligibility, and $15,000,000–$75,000,000 taxable capital phase-out, as well as the post-December 15, 2024 acquisition and available-for-use dates for all SR&ED capital property. Second, CCPCs whose prior-year associated taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000 should annually model the elective three-year average gross revenue phase-out structure to preserve access to the 35% refundable tier. Third, all post-December 15, 2024 SR&ED equipment must be capitalized as depreciable property on the corporate balance sheet rather than expensed in the general ledger, supported by contemporaneous equipment usage logbooks substantiating the 90% ASA test or 50%–90% SUE thresholds. Fourth, Quebec claimants with taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, must transition their accounting systems to the consolidated CRIC regime, capturing newly eligible pre-commercialization regulatory testing and product design expenses while applying the standardized 50% subcontract inclusion rate and employee exclusion threshold. Finally, technical narratives on Form T661 Part 2 (Lines 242, 244, and 246) must be grounded in the binding five-question framework of Northwest Hydraulic and Canafric Inc. v. The King, supported by contemporaneous experimental records and filed together with Schedule 31 well in advance of the strict 18-month statutory reporting bar.
